question: A university IT team runs both real-time AI inference and long-running model training across several clouds and wants an automated balancer. How might an AI-based workload balancer with rule-based pre-scheduling route these two job types, and how can it keep improving its placement choices over time?

If a campus IT group wants an automated multi-cloud balancer for real-time inference and long training jobs, how would rule-based pre-scheduling route each, and how can the balancer improve its placements over time?

A university IT team operates real-time AI inference alongside long-running model training on multiple clouds and wants automated load balancing. How would an AI-based workload balancer using rule-based pre-scheduling direct each of these job types, and how could it continually refine its placement decisions?
answer: Real-time inference jobs are tagged latency-sensitive and preferentially deployed to Google Cloud, the provider with the least latency. Long-running training jobs are forwarded to the providers with the best throughput-to-cost, such as AWS. Reinforcement learning, a variant of Q-learning, updates placement decisions dynamically by adding fresh performance and cost information. Over time the balancer prefers deployments that yield the best aggregate performance for the job type and resource availability.

citation.title: AI and Digital Transformation: Opportunities, Challenges, and Emerging Threats in Technology, Business, and Security

evidence: Real-time inference jobs, for example, were tagged as latency-sensitive and were preferentially deployed to the Google Cloud, the cloud provider with the least latency. With time, the algorithm became attuned to prefer deployments that yielded the best aggregate performance depending on the type of job to be run and the resource availability.

What makes the General AI Attitude Scale (GAAIS) and the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS) each limited as tools for assessing the AI literacy of university educators?
answer: GAAIS captures perceptions and acceptance but under-specifies classroom-proximal competencies, overlooking the technical fluency and ethics-in-use required for effective integration in higher education. MAILS covers technical knowledge, ethical considerations, and practical application, giving a more holistic profile, but it has seen limited validation with university educators. This constrains its transferability to discipline-specific teaching and assessment contexts.

citation.title: AI and Security in China’s Higher Education

evidence: The General AI Attitude Scale (GAAIS) captures perceptions and acceptance, yielding useful indicators of attitudes toward AI (Schepman & Rodway, 2020). However, GAAIS under-specifies classroom-proximal competencies, overlooking technical fluency and ethics-in-use required for effective integration in higher education. … The Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS) provides broader coverage-technical knowledge, ethical considerations, and practical application-offering a more holistic profile of literacy (Long & Magerko, 2020). Yet MAILS has seen limited validation with university educators, constraining transferability to discipline-specific teaching and assessment contexts.

question: What are large language models, and what architecture are they built on?
paraphrases: How are large language models defined, and what architecture underlies them?
What kind of AI models are large language models, and which architecture are they based on?
answer: Large language models are a class of AI models specialized in natural language processing tasks and rely on sequences of tokens. They are essentially deep neural networks with several layers of nodes that map token sequences to vector representations. They are built on transformer architecture, which uses a self-attention approach to weight the relevance of a token in the context of the previous word.

question: In differential privacy, what is the sensitivity of a function, and how is it defined when the function is a machine learning model?
paraphrases: What does sensitivity mean for a function in differential privacy, including when that function is a machine learning model?
How is the sensitivity of a function defined in differential privacy, and what does it mean for a machine learning model?
answer: Sensitivity is the maximum change in output when one record changes between two neighbouring datasets, or the maximum difference one row can make. For a machine learning model, the two datasets differ by one training sample, and sensitivity is the maximum change in the output when one training sample is removed from the training set.

citation.title: Responsible AI

evidence: Sensitivity is the maximum change in output with a change in one record between D1 and D2. Alternatively, it is the maximum difference one row can have as we apply the differential privacy algorithm. … In case of the function being a machine learning model, D1 and D2 are two datasets that differ by one training sample, and the sensitivity would be the maximum change in the output when one training sample is removed from the training set.

question: Why is the sensitivity of a function central to designing differentially private algorithms?
paraphrases: What role does sensitivity play in the design of differentially private algorithms, making it central?

answer: Data bias presents in multiple forms. Sample bias is when a sample dataset does not represent the realities of the environment in which the technology operates. Association bias is when a sample dataset reinforces certain stereotypes present within a culture.
